content: The Trial to Assess Chelation Therapy (TACT) was designed to evaluate the safety and efficacy of ethylene diamine tetra-acetic acid (EDTA) chelation therapy in patients diagnosed with coronary artery disease. The study was sponsored by Mt. Sinai Medical Center in Miami, and the information provided here was sourced from ClinicalTrials.gov on November 19, 2013, under the identifier NCT00044213. Eligibility Criteria Inclusion Criteria: Participants must have experienced a myocardial infarction (heart attack) at least six weeks prior to the start of the study. Exclusion Criteria: Serum creatinine levels exceeding 2.0 mg/dL. Platelet counts below 100,000/µL. Prior chelation therapy within five years before the study's initiation. A history of allergic reactions to EDTA or any components of the therapy. Coronary or carotid revascularization procedures performed within six months prior to the study or planned revascularization procedures. Cigarette smoking within three months prior to the study. Women with childbearing potential. A history of liver disease. Active heart failure or hospitalization for heart failure within six months prior to the study. Diagnoses of other medical conditions that could significantly limit the patient’s survival. Inability to tolerate weekly 500-mL infusions. Study Outcomes Primary Outcomes: Secondary Outcomes: Study Findings Stable Post-Myocardial Infarction Patients: Over a follow-up period of 55 months, the study observed a modest reduction in the risk of adverse cardiovascular outcomes among patients who received chelation therapy. Specifically, 30% of post-myocardial infarction patients who did not receive chelation therapy experienced the primary outcome, compared to 26% of those who underwent chelation therapy (Hazard Ratio [HR]: 0.82; 95% Confidence Interval [CI]: 0.69–0.99; p=0.035). The reduction in risk was significant for most components of the primary outcome, except for total mortality. Despite this moderate improvement, the findings were not sufficient to recommend chelation therapy as a standard treatment for stable post-myocardial infarction patients. Diabetic Post-Myocardial Infarction Patients: The study also analyzed the effects of chelation therapy on cardiovascular outcomes in diabetic patients. Among the 633 diabetic participants in TACT, diabetes was defined as self-reported diabetes, use of diabetes medications, or fasting blood glucose levels above 126 mg/dL at enrollment. Chelation therapy was associated with a significant reduction in the primary endpoint. The primary endpoint occurred in 25% of diabetic patients who received chelation therapy, compared to 38% of those who did not (HR: 0.59; 95% CI: 0.44–0.79; p<0.001). This association remained significant even after adjustments for multiple subgroups (99.4% CI: 0.39–0.88; adjusted p=0.002). Additionally, chelation therapy was linked to a reduction in all-cause mortality; however, this association lost statistical significance after adjustments for multiple subgroups.
